title: Preoperative Assessment & Safety Checklist
summary: Completing the preoperative safety checklist, patient teaching, and handoff before surgery.
steps: Verify patient identity using two identifiers.
Confirm signed, witnessed informed consent matches the scheduled procedure and surgeon.
Assess and document: allergies, current medications, NPO status (nothing by mouth — typically 8h for solids, 6h for non-clear liquids, 2h for clear liquids).
Assess baseline vital signs, height, weight, O2 saturation, pain level.
Complete a full medication reconciliation. Note anticoagulants, antidiabetics, and cardiac medications.
Confirm lab results, imaging, and blood type/screen are available if required.
Remove: jewelry, piercings, nail polish (fingers/toes), contact lenses, hearing aids, dentures, hairpins.
Apply: identification bands, allergy bands, fall risk band as appropriate. Apply anti-embolic stockings or SCDs per order.
Mark surgical site with indelible marker per surgeon order (extremity, laterality).
Administer preoperative medications (antibiotics within 60 min of incision per SCIP guidelines, anxiolytics, etc.).
Perform skin assessment. Clip hair at surgical site only if needed (do NOT shave — increases SSI risk).
Ensure IV access is patent. Complete handoff to OR team using SBAR.
safetyTips: Wrong-site surgery is a never event — confirm site marking with patient while awake.
Antibiotic prophylaxis must be given within 60 minutes of incision — not before, not after.
Shaving the surgical site INCREASES infection risk — use clippers only if hair removal needed.

title: Post-Anesthesia Care Unit (PACU) Assessment
summary: Systematic assessment of the patient immediately following surgery and anesthesia in the PACU.
steps: Receive handoff from anesthesia provider: procedure, anesthetic agents, estimated blood loss, IV fluids given, medications given in OR, any complications.
Immediately assess: airway patency, respiratory rate, SpO2, level of consciousness.
Apply O2 per protocol (most patients receive 2–4L NC or mask initially).
Attach cardiac monitor. Obtain and document vital signs q15 min minimum.
Assess surgical site: dressing integrity, drainage, color, amount.
Assess pain using appropriate scale (NRS, Wong-Baker FACES).
Assess for PONV (postoperative nausea and vomiting) — administer antiemetics per order.
Assess level of consciousness: oriented × 4, emergence agitation vs. normal emergence.
Assess motor/sensory return if regional anesthesia used.
Monitor urine output (catheter if present) — minimum 0.5mL/kg/hr.
ALDRETE SCORE for discharge readiness (each category 0–2): Activity, Respiration, Circulation, Consciousness, O2 Saturation. Score ≥9 required for discharge.
Complete discharge teaching including activity restrictions, pain management, and follow-up instructions.
safetyTips: Airway obstruction post-anesthesia is common — tongue, secretions, laryngospasm. Jaw thrust + suction + airway adjunct.
Emergence agitation: reorient calmly, ensure pain is controlled, rule out hypoxia before sedating.
Malignant hyperthermia can occur post-op — fever + rigidity + tachycardia = call anesthesia STAT.
keyTakeaways: PONV prevention is key to PACU length of stay

title: Surgical Drain Management (JP / Hemovac)
summary: Monitoring and emptying closed-suction surgical drains (Jackson-Pratt and Hemovac).
steps: Perform hand hygiene. Don gloves.
Assess drain site: skin integrity, signs of infection (redness, warmth, purulence), drain security.
JP Drain: bulb should be compressed (creating suction). If expanded, it needs emptying.
Hemovac: flat disk should be compressed. If expanded, needs emptying.
To empty: open the drainage port. Pour contents into graduated container. Measure and record.
Assess drainage: color (serosanguineous → serous is normal progression), amount, and odor.
Compress the drain (JP: squeeze bulb; Hemovac: press flat) before closing the port to reestablish suction.
Wipe port with alcohol swab and close securely.
Secure drain to prevent tension on insertion site — pin to gown, never hang free.
Report: sudden increase in output, bright red output, or output >100mL/hr (possible hemorrhage).
safetyTips: A drain that stops collecting suddenly may be clotted or kinked — assess patency before assuming output has decreased.
Never pull on a drain — if accidentally dislodged, cover site, apply pressure, notify surgeon.
Bright red output suggests active bleeding — do not empty, notify surgeon immediately with volume estimate.
documentation: Amount, color, and character of drainage
keyTakeaways: Keep compressed for suction to work
Bright red or sudden increase = notify surgeon

title: Surgical Site Skin Preparation
summary: Preparing the patient's skin before surgery to reduce surgical site infection (SSI) risk.
equipment: Chlorhexidine gluconate (CHG) scrub cloths or solution
steps: Preoperative shower/bath: instruct patient to shower with CHG soap the night before AND morning of surgery.
Hair removal (in OR or preop): use clippers ONLY — never a razor (razors increase SSI risk). Remove only hair in the operative field.
In OR: surgical prep is performed after positioning.
Apply antimicrobial prep agent (chlorhexidine-alcohol preferred for most sites; iodine for mucous membranes or alcohol-contraindicated areas).
Scrub using friction: start at incision site and work outward in circular or back-and-forth motion. Never return a contaminated applicator to the incision area.
Allow prep to fully dry before draping — chlorhexidine-alcohol is flammable when wet.
Apply sterile drapes to define the surgical field — expose only the operative area.
Eye, ear, or facial surgery: avoid prep agents near eyes/mucous membranes unless specific prep ordered.
safetyTips: Chlorhexidine-alcohol is flammable — allow full drying time before draping to prevent OR fires.
CHG is toxic to the middle ear — never use near the tympanic membrane.
Do NOT use CHG on open wounds or mucous membranes — use iodine-based prep instead.
documentation: Skin condition at site prior to prep
keyTakeaways: Must dry fully before draping — fire risk

title: Intraoperative Patient Positioning
summary: Safely positioning the surgical patient to provide operative exposure while preventing injury.
equipment: Positioning devices (foam pads, gel pads, arm boards, stirrups)
steps: Identify required surgical position based on procedure: supine, prone, lateral, lithotomy, Trendelenburg, reverse Trendelenburg, sitting.
Assess patient: BMI, joint mobility, history of pressure injuries, vascular disease, implants.
Supine: pad all bony prominences (heels, sacrum, elbows). Arms on arm boards at <90° — prevents brachial plexus stretch.
Prone: ensure chest rolls support the thorax — abdomen hangs free to allow ventilation. Head in neutral position. Eyes protected.
Lithotomy: raise both legs simultaneously into stirrups. Level of stirrups and hip flexion must be symmetrical.
Protect eyes in all positions where head is not in neutral — use tape or shields.
Apply safety strap (2 inches above knees) after positioning.
Pad any bony prominence that contacts a hard surface.
After positioning: confirm IV lines/catheters are not kinked. Verify airway is still secure.
Document: position used, padding devices, duration.
safetyTips: Trendelenburg for prolonged time → increased ICP, periorbital edema, airway edema — monitor carefully.
Lithotomy position causes compartment syndrome risk in legs if >2 hours — document start time.
Arms hyperextended on arm boards → brachial plexus injury. Keep at ≤90° from body.
keyTakeaways: Arms ≤90° in supine to prevent brachial plexus injury
